questions.question_text: A function is declared as void update(int& value). What happens to the caller's variable when the function assigns value = 10?

options.text: The caller's variable becomes 10 because it is passed by reference
options.explanation: A reference parameter is an alias for the caller's variable.

options.text: The caller's variable becomes 10 only if it was declared const
options.explanation: const variables cannot be modified at all; constness is the opposite of what allows the change.

options.text: Nothing changes, because C++ always passes arguments by value
options.explanation: C++ passes by value by default, but the & makes this a reference parameter.

options.text: The program fails to compile because references cannot be assigned
options.explanation: Assigning through a reference is legal and modifies the referred object.

options.text: A copy is modified and then copied back when the function returns
options.explanation: That describes copy-in/copy-out semantics, which C++ references do not use.

options.text: The caller's variable is set to the address of the number 10
options.explanation: References do not store addresses that the caller sees; the value 10 is assigned.

questions.question_text: Which header must be included to use std::vector?

options.text: <vector>
options.explanation: std::vector is declared in the <vector> header.

options.text: <array>
options.explanation: <array> declares std::array, a fixed-size container, not std::vector.

options.text: <iostream>, because it includes all standard containers
options.explanation: <iostream> provides stream I/O only; relying on transitive includes is non-portable.

options.text: <list>
options.explanation: <list> declares std::list, a doubly linked list.

options.text: <stdlib.h>
options.explanation: This C header provides general utilities, not C++ containers.

options.text: <algorithm>
options.explanation: <algorithm> provides algorithms such as std::sort, not containers.

questions.question_text: What is the main purpose of a destructor in a C++ class?

options.text: To release resources the object owns when its lifetime ends
options.explanation: Destructors run automatically at end of lifetime to clean up memory, files, locks and similar resources.

options.text: To release resources, but only when delete is called explicitly
options.explanation: Destructors also run automatically for stack objects leaving scope, not only on delete.

options.text: To free the memory of the object itself, so every class must define one
options.explanation: The compiler generates a destructor; a custom one is only needed when the class manages resources.

options.text: To reset all member variables to zero before reuse
options.explanation: Destructors end an object's life; they do not prepare it for reuse.

options.text: To prevent other code from copying the object
options.explanation: Copy control is done with copy constructors and assignment operators, not destructors.

options.text: To create a backup copy of the object before it is removed

questions.question_text: Given int arr[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};, what does arr[5] access?

options.text: Memory past the end of the array, which is undefined behaviour
options.explanation: Valid indices are 0 to 4; index 5 is out of bounds.

options.text: The last element, 5, because arrays are indexed from 1
options.explanation: C++ arrays are zero-indexed, so the last element is arr[4].

options.text: It throws an std::out_of_range exception automatically
options.explanation: Built-in arrays do no bounds checking; only functions like std::vector::at throw.

options.text: It returns 0 because unused slots are zero-initialised
options.explanation: There is no sixth slot; reading past the end is undefined.

options.text: The compiler always rejects it with an error
options.explanation: Compilers usually cannot detect this; it compiles and misbehaves at runtime.

options.text: It wraps around and returns the first element, 1
options.explanation: C++ arrays do not wrap around.

questions.question_text: What does the keyword const mean in the declaration const int max_users = 100;?

options.text: max_users cannot be modified after initialisation
options.explanation: const makes the variable read-only after it is initialised.

options.text: max_users cannot be modified, but it can be left uninitialised
options.explanation: A const object must be initialised when declared.

options.text: max_users is stored in a special constant memory that is faster to access
options.explanation: const is about mutability, not a guaranteed storage location or speed.

options.text: max_users is shared between all source files automatically
options.explanation: Namespace-scope const variables have internal linkage by default, the opposite of shared.

options.text: max_users can only be read inside the function where it is declared
options.explanation: const does not restrict scope; scope depends on where it is declared.

options.text: max_users is evaluated again each time it is used
options.explanation: const values are fixed after initialisation.

questions.question_text: A class owns a raw pointer allocated with new in its constructor and deletes it in its destructor. It has no copy constructor or copy assignment. What is the risk when an object is copied?

options.text: Both copies delete the same pointer, causing a double free
options.explanation: The implicit copy constructor copies the pointer value, so two destructors free the same memory.

options.text: The copy gets a new allocation but leaks the original memory
options.explanation: The implicit copy does not allocate; it shares the pointer, which leads to a double free.

options.text: There is no risk because the compiler generates a deep copy automatically
options.explanation: Compiler-generated copies are member-wise (shallow) for raw pointers.

options.text: The copy fails to compile because classes with destructors cannot be copied
options.explanation: A user-declared destructor does not delete the copy operations.

options.text: The pointer in the copy is set to nullptr automatically
options.explanation: The implicit copy constructor copies the pointer value unchanged.

options.text: Only performance suffers, because copying a pointer is slow
options.explanation: Copying a pointer is cheap; the problem is shared ownership.

questions.question_text: Which smart pointer should you use for an object that has exactly one owner and must be destroyed when that owner goes out of scope?

options.text: std::unique_ptr
options.explanation: unique_ptr models exclusive ownership with no reference-counting overhead.

options.text: std::shared_ptr with a use count of one
options.explanation: shared_ptr works, but adds reference counting and allows accidental sharing.

options.text: std::weak_ptr, because it does not affect the object's lifetime
options.explanation: weak_ptr does not own anything; it observes an object owned by shared_ptr.

options.text: std::auto_ptr, the standard choice for single ownership
options.explanation: auto_ptr was deprecated in C++11 and removed in C++17.

options.text: A raw pointer, since smart pointers are only needed for arrays
options.explanation: Raw owning pointers lose automatic cleanup and exception safety.

options.text: std::reference_wrapper
options.explanation: reference_wrapper wraps a reference; it does not own or destroy objects.

questions.question_text: Why is it important to declare the destructor virtual in a base class that will be used polymorphically?

options.text: So deleting a derived object through a base pointer runs the derived destructor
options.explanation: Without a virtual destructor, delete through a base pointer is undefined behaviour.

options.text: So derived classes are forced to define their own destructors
options.explanation: A virtual destructor does not force derived classes to define one.

options.text: To make the destructor run faster through the vtable
options.explanation: Virtual dispatch adds a small cost; the reason is correctness, not speed.

options.text: So the base class cannot be instantiated on its own
options.explanation: That is done with pure virtual functions, not a virtual destructor.

options.text: To allow the object to be copied safely between base and derived types
options.explanation: Copying and slicing are unrelated to virtual destructors.

options.text: Because constructors must also be declared virtual in that case
options.explanation: Constructors cannot be virtual in C++.

questions.question_text: You call std::vector<int>::push_back many times. Why can a pointer you previously took to an element become invalid?

options.text: The vector may reallocate to a larger buffer and move its elements
options.explanation: When capacity is exceeded, elements move to new memory, invalidating pointers and iterators.

options.text: Pointers are only invalidated when you call reserve()
options.explanation: reserve can invalidate pointers too, but push_back alone can trigger reallocation.

options.text: Pointers never become invalid in a vector; only iterators do
options.explanation: Reallocation invalidates pointers, references and iterators.

options.text: push_back sorts the elements, so the pointer refers to a different value
options.explanation: push_back appends; it does not sort.

options.text: The vector compacts memory every time an element is added
options.explanation: Vectors only reallocate when capacity runs out.

options.text: push_back copies the whole vector to the stack
options.explanation: Elements are stored on the heap; the vector is not copied to the stack.

questions.question_text: What does the following loop do: for (const auto& item : items) { ... }?

options.text: Iterates over items without copying elements and without allowing modification
options.explanation: const auto& binds a read-only reference to each element.

options.text: Iterates over items without copying, and allows each element to be modified
options.explanation: const prevents modification through the reference.

options.text: Copies every element first, then iterates over the copies
options.explanation: A reference type avoids copies; only auto without & copies.

options.text: Iterates over items in reverse order
options.explanation: A range-based for loop goes from begin() to end().

options.text: Iterates only over items that are themselves const
options.explanation: The const applies to the loop reference, not a filter on elements.

options.text: Creates a new container containing only the elements processed
options.explanation: The loop does not create a container.

questions.question_text: A function returns a large std::vector by value: std::vector<Record> load(). In modern C++, why is this usually efficient?

options.text: Copy elision or move semantics avoid copying the elements
options.explanation: Return value optimisation constructs the result in place, or the vector is moved, which only transfers its buffer.

options.text: Because the compiler passes the vector by reference behind the scenes in all cases
options.explanation: Copy elision is guaranteed only for prvalues; otherwise a move is used, not an implicit reference.

options.text: It is not efficient; you should always return a pointer to a heap vector instead
options.explanation: Returning by value is idiomatic and efficient since C++11.

options.text: Because std::vector stores its elements on the stack of the caller
options.explanation: Vector elements live on the heap.

options.text: Because the elements are copied lazily only when accessed
options.explanation: C++ vectors do not use copy-on-write.

options.text: Because std::vector is reference-counted like std::shared_ptr

questions.question_text: In a multi-threaded program, two threads increment a shared int counter with counter++. What is the correct fix with the least overhead for this single variable?

options.text: Make it std::atomic<int> and use counter++ or fetch_add
options.explanation: Atomic operations make the increment indivisible without a full mutex.

options.text: Declare the counter volatile so both threads see the latest value
options.explanation: volatile does not provide atomicity or ordering guarantees between threads in C++.

options.text: No fix is needed because ++ on an int is a single CPU instruction
options.explanation: counter++ is a read-modify-write that can interleave, losing updates.

options.text: Call std::this_thread::yield() before each increment
options.explanation: Yielding changes scheduling but does not prevent data races.

options.text: Use a std::shared_mutex and take a shared lock for the increment
options.explanation: A shared lock allows concurrent writers, so the race remains.

options.text: Move the counter into thread_local storage
options.explanation: thread_local gives each thread its own counter, so they no longer share a total.

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of std::move in the expression target = std::move(source);?

options.text: It casts source to an rvalue so a move assignment can be selected
options.explanation: std::move itself moves nothing; it enables overloads that transfer resources.

options.text: It moves the data immediately and guarantees source is empty afterwards
options.explanation: The type's move operation decides what happens; source is left valid but unspecified.

options.text: It performs a faster deep copy and leaves source unchanged
options.explanation: A move typically steals resources and may change source.

options.text: It moves source to a different memory location on the heap
options.explanation: std::move does not relocate objects in memory.

options.text: It locks source so other threads cannot access it during assignment
options.explanation: std::move has nothing to do with thread synchronisation.

options.text: It is only valid for built-in types like int and double
options.explanation: It is mainly useful for types that own resources, such as strings and containers.

questions.question_text: You see a template function that only compiles for some types and produces long, confusing error messages for others. Which C++20 feature best expresses the type requirements?

options.text: Concepts with a requires clause
options.explanation: Concepts state requirements directly and give clearer diagnostics.

options.text: static_assert inside the function body
options.explanation: static_assert improves messages but does not take part in overload resolution as concepts do.

options.text: Virtual functions in a common base class
options.explanation: That is runtime polymorphism; it does not constrain template parameters.

options.text: The auto keyword for every parameter
options.explanation: Abbreviated templates still need constraints to restrict types.

options.text: Macros that check the type name as a string
Explicit template instantiation for all allowed types
options.explanation: That controls code generation, not constraint checking for callers.

questions.question_text: Profiling shows a hot loop over a std::vector<Particle> where only the position field is read, and each Particle is 128 bytes. What change is most likely to improve cache performance?

options.text: Store positions in a separate contiguous array (structure of arrays)
options.explanation: Packing only the needed data together makes better use of each cache line.

options.text: Mark the loop variable const so the compiler can cache it
options.explanation: const may help optimisation, but it does not change memory layout or cache use.

options.text: Switch to std::list so elements can be accessed independently
options.explanation: Linked lists scatter nodes in memory and hurt cache locality.

options.text: Make Particle's members virtual to allow faster dispatch
options.explanation: Virtual functions add a vtable pointer and do not help data access.

options.text: Allocate each Particle separately with new for better alignment
options.explanation: Separate allocations scatter objects and reduce locality.

options.text: Increase the vector's capacity with reserve before the loop
options.explanation: reserve avoids reallocations but does not change the layout read by the loop.

questions.question_text: In most CAD programs, what is the main difference between a 2D drawing and a 3D model?

options.text: A 3D model represents geometry with depth, while a 2D drawing shows flat views
options.explanation: 3D models hold full spatial geometry that 2D views are projected from.

options.text: A 3D model is several 2D drawings stacked on separate layers, while a 2D drawing uses only one layer
options.explanation: Layers organise content; they do not create depth.

options.text: 2D drawings are always more accurate than 3D models
options.explanation: Accuracy depends on how the geometry is defined, not on dimension.

options.text: 3D models cannot be dimensioned or printed
options.explanation: 3D models can be annotated and used to produce printed drawings.

options.text: 2D drawings can only contain straight lines
options.explanation: 2D drawings include arcs, circles, splines and text.

options.text: There is no difference except the file extension
options.explanation: The data and use are fundamentally different.

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of layers in a CAD drawing?

options.text: To organise objects so they can be shown, hidden or styled as groups
options.explanation: Layers group related objects such as walls, dimensions or electrical items.

options.text: To organise objects, but each object can belong to several layers at once
options.explanation: In typical CAD tools an object belongs to exactly one layer.

options.text: To store different versions of the same drawing
options.explanation: Versions are handled by file history or revision control, not layers.

options.text: To increase the resolution of the drawing when printed
options.explanation: Print resolution is a plot setting, not a layer feature.

options.text: To lock the drawing so only one user can edit it
options.explanation: File locking is separate from layer organisation.

options.text: To convert a 2D drawing into a 3D model
options.explanation: Layers do not add a third dimension.

questions.question_text: You need to draw a line exactly 50 mm long at 30 degrees. What is the most reliable method in CAD?

options.text: Enter the length and angle numerically or with polar coordinates
options.explanation: Typed input gives exact geometry rather than approximate mouse picks.

options.text: Draw it with the mouse and check the length with a measure tool afterwards
options.explanation: Measuring after drawing finds errors but does not create exact geometry.

options.text: Zoom in very far before clicking so the mouse position is precise enough
options.explanation: Zooming improves visual accuracy but never guarantees exact values.

options.text: Draw a longer line and scale the whole drawing until it looks right
options.explanation: Scaling everything distorts the other geometry.

options.text: Use the text tool to label the line 50 mm
options.explanation: A label does not change the actual geometry.

options.text: Turn on grid display, which forces lines to exact angles
options.explanation: Grid display alone does not constrain angles; snap settings would be needed.

questions.question_text: What does the object snap feature (for example endpoint or midpoint snap) do?

options.text: Locks the cursor to exact points on existing geometry
options.explanation: Snaps let you start or end objects precisely at defined points.

options.text: Locks the cursor to grid points only
options.explanation: That is grid snap; object snap uses points on existing objects.

options.text: Automatically connects any lines that are close to each other
options.explanation: Snaps help placement; they do not join separate objects.

options.text: Rotates the view to look at the selected point
options.explanation: View rotation is a navigation feature.

options.text: Creates a copy of the object at the cursor position
Checks the drawing for errors before saving

questions.question_text: Why do engineers often draw at full scale (1:1) in CAD model space?

options.text: Because real-world sizes are kept, and scaling is applied only when printing or in layouts
options.explanation: Full scale keeps dimensions true and simplifies measurement.

options.text: Because plotters and printers can only output drawings at 1:1, so other scales cause printing errors
options.explanation: Drawings can be plotted at any scale.

options.text: Because CAD software cannot store very large or very small numbers
options.explanation: CAD handles a wide range of sizes; the reason is clarity, not limitations.

options.text: Because it makes the file size smaller
options.explanation: Scale has little effect on file size.

options.text: Because dimensions are not allowed in scaled drawings
options.explanation: Scaled layouts still show correct dimensions.

options.text: Because 1:1 drawings do not need units

questions.question_text: In a parametric 3D CAD model, what is a sketch constraint such as "parallel" or "equal"?

options.text: A geometric rule that keeps relationships between sketch entities when dimensions change
options.explanation: Constraints preserve design intent as the model is edited.

options.text: A dimension that fixes the exact length of a single line so it cannot change when the sketch is edited
options.explanation: That is a dimensional constraint, not a geometric one.

options.text: A setting that prevents anyone from editing the sketch
options.explanation: Constraints define relationships; they are not permissions.

options.text: A note that appears on the printed drawing
options.explanation: Annotations are separate from sketch constraints.

options.text: A material property used in stress simulation

options.text: A layer filter that hides some lines

questions.question_text: A part's feature tree shows a hole feature that fails after you edit an earlier extrusion. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The hole referenced a face or edge that changed or no longer exists
options.explanation: Parent-child references break when earlier geometry changes.

options.text: The hole's diameter is larger than the default allowed by the software

options.text: Features always fail after any edit and must be redrawn every time
The file was saved in a newer version of the software

options.text: The hole was drawn on the wrong layer
options.explanation: Layers do not determine feature success in parametric solid modelling.

options.text: The material of the part was not assigned
options.explanation: Material assignment does not affect feature regeneration.

questions.question_text: What is the advantage of using blocks or reusable components for repeated items such as bolts or doors?

options.text: One definition is reused, so editing it updates every instance
options.explanation: Blocks keep drawings consistent and files smaller.

options.text: Each copy becomes independent, so you can edit them individually without affecting others
options.explanation: That describes exploded copies; blocks are linked to one definition.

options.text: Blocks are only for decoration and cannot be scaled or rotated
options.explanation: Block instances can be scaled, rotated and mirrored.

options.text: Blocks make the drawing open faster on other computers only
options.explanation: The main benefits are consistency and easy updates.

options.text: Blocks automatically generate a bill of materials in every CAD program

options.text: Blocks convert 2D geometry into 3D parts
options.explanation: Blocks can be 2D or 3D; they do not convert dimensions.

questions.question_text: You are creating an assembly. Which approach keeps a bracket correctly positioned relative to a plate when the plate's size changes?

options.text: Use mates or constraints that reference the plate's faces and edges
options.explanation: Mates keep relationships when parts change.

options.text: Place the bracket at fixed coordinates matching the plate's current corner
options.explanation: Fixed coordinates do not follow the plate when it changes.

options.text: Merge the bracket and plate into one part so they cannot move

options.text: Increase the assembly's tolerance setting

options.text: Lock the bracket so it cannot be selected

questions.question_text: When preparing a 2D drawing from a 3D model, why should views be linked to the model rather than drawn separately?

options.text: Linked views update automatically when the model changes
options.explanation: Associative views stay consistent with the model.

options.text: Linked views update, but only dimensions update while geometry stays fixed
options.explanation: Both geometry and model dimensions update.

options.text: Separate drawings are always more accurate than projected views
options.explanation: Projections from the model are exact; manual drawing risks mismatch.

options.text: Linked views produce smaller printed sheets
options.explanation: Sheet size is set by the drawing template.

options.text: Linked views do not need a title block
Linked views remove the need for dimensions
options.explanation: Drawings still need dimensions for manufacturing.

questions.question_text: A complex model is slow to rebuild. Which practice most effectively improves rebuild performance without losing design intent?

options.text: Simplify the feature tree by removing redundant features and avoiding unnecessary references
Suppress all fillets and chamfers permanently, since they are never needed for manufacturing drawings

options.text: Convert the model to a dumb solid after every change

options.text: Increase the display resolution of curved surfaces

options.text: Save the file more often

options.text: Move all sketches onto a single plane
options.explanation: Sketch plane choice should follow design intent, not performance.

questions.question_text: A part will be manufactured by CNC machining. What modelling decision best supports manufacturability?

options.text: Add internal corner radii that match available cutter sizes
options.explanation: Milling tools cannot produce sharp internal corners.

options.text: Use sharp internal corners and let the machinist decide the radius
options.explanation: Leaving this undefined causes rework and mismatched expectations.

options.text: Make wall thickness as thin as possible to save material
options.explanation: Very thin walls vibrate and deform during machining.

options.text: Model all holes at non-standard diameters for precision
options.explanation: Standard drill sizes reduce cost and lead time.

options.text: Use freeform surfaces everywhere for better appearance
options.explanation: Freeform surfaces increase machining time and cost.

questions.question_text: In a top-down assembly design, what is the main risk of creating many in-context references between parts?

options.text: Parts become dependent on each other, causing rebuild failures and circular references
options.explanation: In-context links are powerful but fragile when overused.

options.text: Only the assembly file becomes larger on disk, with no effect on rebuilds or on the individual parts

options.text: In-context references are always forbidden in professional CAD work

options.text: JPEG

questions.question_text: A design must allow assembly of mass-produced parts that vary within tolerances. What should the CAD drawing specify to control fit?

Only nominal dimensions on every feature, with a general note asking the workshop to make the parts fit

The total weight of each part
The CAD software version used to create the model

options.text: To indicate how much reagent to add

options.explanation: Conditioning prepares the sorbent for sample loading.

options.text: To elute any analyte already on the sorbent before loading the sample onto the cartridge
options.explanation: Elution happens after loading and washing.

options.text: To remove the analyte from the sorbent permanently
options.explanation: Conditioning occurs before the analyte is introduced.

options.text: To dry the sample completely
options.explanation: Drying can happen later, not during conditioning.

options.text: To filter out particles from the solvent
To weigh the cartridge before use
options.explanation: Weighing is not part of conditioning.

questions.question_text: A method requires microwave digestion of a soil sample before metal analysis. What is the main goal?

options.text: To dissolve the matrix and release the metals into solution
options.explanation: Digestion converts the sample into a measurable solution.

options.text: To dry the soil fully at high temperature without changing its chemical composition
options.explanation: Drying and digestion are different steps.

options.text: To remove all metals so the background is clean
options.explanation: Digestion releases the metals for measurement.

options.text: To grind the soil into a fine powder
To kill microorganisms only
To separate the soil into layers by density
options.explanation: Density separation is a different technique.

questions.question_text: A sample must be stored before analysis of volatile organic compounds. Which practice is best?

options.text: Use sealed containers with no headspace and refrigerate
Use sealed containers but leave headspace for expansion
options.explanation: Headspace allows volatiles to partition out of the sample.

options.text: Store in open containers so the sample stays at equilibrium with air
Freeze and thaw the sample several times to stabilise it
Add more solvent to replace losses later
options.explanation: Losses cannot be corrected this way.

options.text: Store at room temperature in plastic bags
options.explanation: Plastic bags are permeable and may adsorb analytes.

questions.question_text: Why is a procedural blank prepared alongside the samples?

options.text: To detect contamination introduced by reagents, equipment or handling
options.explanation: Blanks show the contribution of the preparation process.

options.text: To measure the maximum concentration the method can detect
options.explanation: Blanks help estimate detection limits but do not measure the maximum.

options.text: Blanks are only needed when the samples look contaminated
To provide a reference sample with known analyte concentration
options.explanation: That is a reference material or spiked sample.

options.text: To calibrate the balance
To replace a failed sample in the batch

questions.question_text: Spike recovery for an analyte is 65% in a complex matrix but 98% in clean solvent. What is the most likely issue?

options.text: Matrix effects or losses during preparation that depend on the sample matrix
options.explanation: Low recovery only in the matrix points to matrix-related losses.

options.text: The calibration standards were prepared incorrectly, which affects every result in the batch
options.explanation: Calibration errors would also lower the clean-solvent recovery.

options.text: The method is fine because the solvent recovery is acceptable
options.explanation: Recovery in the real matrix is what matters.

options.text: The balance needs recalibration
options.explanation: Weighing errors would affect both results.

options.text: The sample was too homogeneous
options.explanation: Homogeneity does not cause low recovery.

options.text: The spike was added after analysis
options.explanation: That would give no recovery at all.

questions.question_text: To reduce matrix effects in LC-MS sample preparation, which approach is most robust?

options.text: Use an isotopically labelled internal standard added before extraction
options.explanation: It tracks losses and ionisation effects for the analyte.

options.text: Add the internal standard just before injection so it is not lost during extraction
options.explanation: That corrects instrument variation, not preparation losses.

options.text: Dilute every sample tenfold regardless of sensitivity
options.explanation: Dilution can help but may push analytes below detection limits.

options.text: Increase the injection volume
Use only clean solvent standards for calibration
Skip filtration to keep all analyte in the sample

questions.question_text: A trace metal method gives high blank values. Which change is most effective?

options.text: Use acid-cleaned plastic labware and high-purity reagents
options.explanation: Contamination from glassware and reagents is a common source.

options.text: Use standard laboratory glassware but rinse it twice with tap water
Subtract the blank value and ignore the source
options.explanation: High, variable blanks raise detection limits and must be controlled.

options.text: Increase the sample mass and keep everything else unchanged
options.explanation: This may help signal but does not fix contamination.

options.text: Store samples in metal containers
Prepare samples on an open bench near a ventilation outlet

questions.question_text: When subsampling a heterogeneous granular material, which approach best reduces sampling error?

options.text: Reduce particle size and use a riffle splitter or similar division method
options.explanation: Smaller particles and proper division improve representativeness.

options.text: Take one large scoop from the top of the container, since a big portion is always representative
options.explanation: Segregation makes the top layer unrepresentative.

options.text: Take one small portion; random chance makes it representative
options.explanation: Small portions of heterogeneous material vary widely.

options.text: Shake the container and pour out the first portion
Choose the portion that looks most typical
Dissolve only the large particles
options.explanation: That excludes part of the sample.

questions.question_text: An analyte degrades at room temperature in the prepared extract. What is the best control measure?

options.text: Keep extracts chilled and protected, and validate the maximum holding time
options.explanation: Stability data defines how long extracts remain valid.

options.text: Keep extracts chilled and protected, then analyse them whenever it is convenient for the lab
options.explanation: Without a validated holding time, degradation may still occur.

options.text: Add more analyte to the extract to compensate
Store extracts in clear glass in sunlight
Use larger volumes so degradation is less noticeable
options.explanation: Degradation is proportional, not reduced by volume.

options.text: Evaporate extracts to dryness and store indefinitely
options.explanation: Drying may cause losses and needs validation.

questions.question_text: In chromatography data software, what does the retention time of a peak represent?

options.text: The time from injection until the peak's maximum is detected
options.explanation: Retention time helps identify compounds under fixed conditions.

options.text: The width of the peak measured at its base, from where it leaves to where it returns to baseline
The concentration of the compound
options.explanation: Concentration is derived from peak area or height.

options.text: The total run time of the method
options.explanation: Run time is the whole analysis duration.

options.text: The time the sample stays in the vial
The time needed to calibrate the instrument

questions.question_text: Which result is usually used to quantify a compound in a chromatogram?

options.text: The peak area compared with a calibration curve
options.explanation: Area is proportional to amount over the calibrated range.

options.text: The peak's retention time compared with a standard
options.explanation: Retention time identifies; it does not quantify.

options.text: The colour of the peak in the display
options.explanation: Display colours carry no quantitative meaning.

options.text: The number of peaks in the chromatogram
options.explanation: Peak count does not give concentration.

options.text: The baseline noise level
options.explanation: Noise affects detection limits, not quantity.

options.text: The column temperature

questions.question_text: What is a processing method in chromatography software?

options.text: Settings that tell the software how to integrate, identify and quantify peaks
options.explanation: Processing methods turn raw data into results.

options.text: Settings that control the pump flow, column temperature and detector during the run
options.explanation: Those belong to the instrument (acquisition) method.

options.text: A report template only
options.explanation: Report templates format results; processing generates them.

options.text: A list of users allowed to log in
The backup schedule for data files
The order of samples in the autosampler

questions.question_text: What is a sequence (or sample set) in chromatography software?

options.text: An ordered list of injections with sample names, vial positions and methods
A list of the peaks and retention times expected to appear in each chromatogram
A calibration curve with several points
options.explanation: Calibration levels are part of a sequence but not the same thing.

options.text: The audit trail of changes
The column installation record
The order in which reports are printed
options.explanation: Printing order is not the sequence.

questions.question_text: Why should raw chromatography data be kept even after the final report is printed?

options.text: Because results may need reprocessing, review or audit later
options.explanation: Raw data supports traceability and compliance.

options.text: Because raw data is required only if the report has errors
Raw data can be deleted once the report is signed
options.explanation: Deleting raw data breaks data integrity requirements.

options.text: Raw data is needed to print colour charts
Raw data improves instrument performance
options.explanation: Stored data does not affect the instrument.

options.text: Raw data takes up no storage space

questions.question_text: A peak is integrated with a baseline that cuts through a neighbouring peak. What is the best action?

options.text: Adjust integration parameters or events in the processing method and document the change
options.explanation: Method-level changes are consistent and traceable.

options.text: Manually redraw that one baseline in the result without recording the reason for the change
options.explanation: Undocumented manual integration is a data integrity risk.

options.text: Ignore it because integration errors cancel out over many samples
Delete the neighbouring peak from the data
Increase the detector wavelength until the peaks merge
options.explanation: Changing acquisition to hide problems is inappropriate.

options.text: Report only the retention time instead of area

questions.question_text: What does an audit trail in chromatography software record?

options.text: Who changed what, when, and often why
options.explanation: Audit trails provide traceability for regulated work.

options.text: Only the date each sample was run
options.explanation: Audit trails also record changes and users.

options.text: Only errors produced by the instrument
The chemical composition of each sample
The amount of solvent consumed
options.explanation: Consumption is not part of the audit trail.

options.text: The physical location of the instrument

questions.question_text: A calibration curve has R² = 0.999, but the lowest standard is 30% off its nominal value. What should you conclude?

options.text: The fit may hide poor accuracy at low concentrations; check residuals and weighting
options.explanation: R² alone does not prove accuracy across the range.

options.text: The curve is acceptable because R² is above 0.995, which proves accuracy at every level
options.explanation: A high R² can hide large relative errors at low levels.

options.text: R² measures accuracy directly, so the low standard must be wrong
options.explanation: R² measures fit, not accuracy at each level.

options.text: Delete the low standard so the curve looks better
options.explanation: Removing points without justification is inappropriate.

options.text: Use the highest standard only
Increase the run time
options.explanation: Run time does not affect calibration accuracy.

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of system suitability tests in a chromatography sequence?

options.text: To confirm the system performs adequately before and during sample analysis
options.explanation: Tests check resolution, precision, tailing and similar criteria.

options.text: To calibrate the detector wavelength and lamp energy at the start of each sequence
They are optional checks run only if results look wrong
options.explanation: They are usually required before sample results are accepted.

options.text: To test the analyst's knowledge
To clean the column between runs
To check the user's access rights

questions.question_text: Why should users have different roles (for example analyst, reviewer, administrator) in chromatography software?

options.text: To separate duties so no single user can create, change and approve data unchecked
To give every user full access to all functions, but record their actions in the audit trail
options.explanation: Tracking alone does not separate duties.

options.text: Roles only matter in large laboratories
options.explanation: Integrity requirements apply regardless of lab size.

options.text: To make the software run faster
To limit the number of instruments that can be connected
To reduce data storage costs

questions.question_text: During review, you notice a sample was reprocessed several times and only the last result was reported. What is the main concern?

options.text: Possible testing into compliance; all reprocessing must be justified and reviewed
options.explanation: Repeated reprocessing without justification is a data integrity red flag.

options.text: The software may have slowed down from repeated processing, so the system needs maintenance
Reprocessing is always forbidden
options.explanation: Justified reprocessing is acceptable when documented.

options.text: The sample must be destroyed
options.explanation: Destroying samples is not the remedy.

options.text: Only the first result should ever be reported
options.explanation: The valid result depends on justification.

options.text: The instrument needs requalification
options.explanation: Reprocessing does not imply instrument failure.

questions.question_text: A laboratory moves to a networked chromatography data system. What is the key validation consideration?

options.text: Demonstrate that data is captured, stored and secured correctly across the network with tested backup and restore
options.explanation: Computerised system validation covers integrity and recovery.

options.text: Validate that the software installs without errors on each client, since the network vendor is certified
options.explanation: Installation checks are only one part of validation.

options.text: Network systems need no validation if the vendor is certified
options.explanation: The user is responsible for validation in its intended use.

options.text: Validate only that reports print correctly
Validation is required only for standalone systems
Validate only the oldest instrument

questions.question_text: Peaks drift to later retention times across a long sequence. How should the software be configured to identify peaks reliably?

options.text: Use relative retention to an internal or reference peak, or update retention times from bracketing standards
Widen the retention time window as much as possible so that every drifting peak always stays inside its own window
options.explanation: Very wide windows risk misidentifying neighbouring peaks.

options.text: Ignore retention time and identify peaks by size only
Reprocess with a shorter run time
Disable peak identification and report all peaks as unknown
options.explanation: That avoids the problem instead of solving it.

options.text: Change the column temperature in the processing method

questions.question_text: Two co-eluting compounds share one peak. Which software capability can help assess this?

options.text: Peak purity analysis using spectral data from a diode array or mass detector
options.explanation: Spectral comparison across the peak detects co-elution.

options.text: Increasing the integration threshold so that only the larger of the two compounds is reported
options.explanation: Thresholds change detection, not purity assessment.

options.text: Assuming one compound because the peak is symmetric
Changing the report font
Adding a second calibration level
Exporting the chromatogram to a spreadsheet

questions.question_text: An analyst asks for permission to delete failed injections from the sequence to save space. What is the correct response?

options.text: Keep them; failed injections are part of the record and must be investigated or documented
Delete them if they are older than one month, since only valid results must be kept as records
options.explanation: Retention rules apply to all data generated.

options.text: Delete them, because only valid results matter
options.explanation: All data generated must be retained.

options.text: Move them to a USB drive and delete the originals
Rename them as blanks
Delete them after the reviewer signs

questions.question_text: What is the main goal of continuous integration (CI)?

options.text: To merge code changes often and automatically build and test them
options.explanation: Frequent automated checks find integration problems early.

options.text: To merge code changes once per release after manual testing
To deploy every change directly to production without tests
options.explanation: That is risky; CI is about verifying changes.

options.text: To write documentation automatically
To replace version control
To reduce the number of developers needed

questions.question_text: In a CI pipeline, what usually triggers a build?

options.text: A push or pull request to the repository
options.explanation: Pipelines run automatically on code changes.

options.text: A manual request from the project manager only
options.explanation: Pipelines can be manual, but CI typically runs on changes.

options.text: The end of each working day only
options.explanation: Nightly builds exist but are not the CI standard.

options.text: Opening the IDE
options.explanation: Local IDE actions do not trigger the CI server.

options.text: Creating a new user account
Changing the README file only
options.explanation: README changes can trigger CI, but that is not the usual trigger definition.

questions.question_text: What is a build artifact in CI/CD?

options.text: A packaged output of the build, such as a binary, container image or archive
options.explanation: Artifacts are deployed or used later.

options.text: The source code files in the repository that are checked out at the start of every build
options.explanation: Source code is the input, not the output.

options.text: A failed test report only
options.explanation: Reports may be stored, but artifacts are build outputs.

options.text: A comment on a pull request
The configuration of the CI server
A temporary file deleted after compiling
options.explanation: Artifacts are kept for later stages.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?

options.text: Delivery keeps code always releasable with a manual release step; deployment releases automatically
options.explanation: Continuous deployment removes the manual approval.

options.text: Delivery deploys automatically to production; deployment only builds and stores artifacts for later release
They are identical terms
options.explanation: They differ in whether release to production is automatic.

options.text: Delivery is for mobile apps, deployment for web apps
Delivery means sending code by email
Deployment means installing CI tools

questions.question_text: Why should a CI pipeline fail if unit tests fail?

options.text: To stop broken code from progressing to later stages
options.explanation: Failing fast protects the main branch and deployments.

options.text: To notify the team, while still deploying the build
Tests are informational only and should not block the pipeline
options.explanation: Unblocking failures defeats the purpose of CI.

options.text: To force developers to rewrite all tests
options.explanation: The goal is to fix the issue.

options.text: To save cloud costs only
options.explanation: Cost is not the main reason.

options.text: Because CI tools cannot handle test results
options.explanation: CI tools handle test results well.

questions.question_text: Secrets like API keys are needed in a pipeline. What is the safest approach?

options.text: Store them in the CI system's secret store and inject them at runtime
options.explanation: Secrets stay out of the repository and logs.

options.text: Store them in a private repository file that only the team can read
options.explanation: Repositories are copied and kept in history.

options.text: Hard-code them in the pipeline file because pipelines are private
options.explanation: Pipeline files are code and often widely visible.

options.text: Print them in logs so failures can be debugged
Email them to each developer
Store them in the build artifact

questions.question_text: Pipelines take 40 minutes and developers wait for feedback. Which change usually gives the biggest improvement?

options.text: Run independent jobs in parallel and cache dependencies
options.explanation: Parallelism and caching reduce wall-clock time.

options.text: Remove all integration tests and keep unit tests
options.explanation: This speeds up feedback but loses coverage.

options.text: Run the pipeline only once per week
options.explanation: Less frequent feedback makes integration problems worse.

options.text: Use a larger monitor for viewing logs
options.explanation: Displays do not affect pipeline time.

options.text: Add more manual approval steps
Rebuild every dependency from source on each run

questions.question_text: What is the benefit of building the artifact once and promoting the same artifact through test, staging and production?

options.text: The tested artifact is exactly what reaches production
It reduces storage, but each environment should still rebuild for safety
Each environment should always have its own separately built artifact
options.explanation: Separate builds can differ even from the same code.

options.text: It removes the need for tests
It makes configuration unnecessary
It ensures every developer uses the same IDE

questions.question_text: A flaky test fails randomly about 5% of the time. What is the best way to handle it?

options.text: Quarantine or fix it quickly, and track the root cause
options.explanation: Flaky tests erode trust in the pipeline.

options.text: Automatically retry the pipeline until it passes, with no follow-up
Ignore it because 95% success is good enough
options.explanation: Teams then start ignoring real failures.

options.text: Delete all tests in that file
Run the test only on Fridays
Increase the timeout of every test
options.explanation: Timeouts may not be the cause.

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of environment-specific configuration in CD?

options.text: To use the same artifact with different settings for each environment
To build a different version of the code for each environment
options.explanation: Code should be the same; configuration varies.

options.text: To store all passwords in the source code for each environment
options.explanation: Secrets should be in secure stores.

options.text: To decide which developers can deploy
To reduce the number of environments
To make tests run faster
options.explanation: Configuration may change test behaviour but that is not its purpose.

questions.question_text: Your team wants zero-downtime releases with the ability to roll back quickly. Which strategy is most suitable?

options.text: Blue-green deployment with traffic switching between two environments
options.explanation: Traffic moves to the new version and can switch back.

options.text: Rolling deployment that replaces instances one by one with no health checks between steps
options.explanation: Health checks are needed to catch failures and roll back safely.

options.text: Stop the old version, deploy the new one, then restart
Deploy directly over production files during working hours
Deploy only on weekends when traffic is lower
options.explanation: Timing reduces impact but does not remove downtime.

options.text: Ask users to clear their cache after each release
options.explanation: This does not address server downtime.

questions.question_text: A canary release sends 5% of traffic to the new version. What should decide whether to continue the rollout?

options.text: Automated comparison of error rates, latency and business metrics against the stable version
options.explanation: Objective metrics show whether the canary is healthy.

options.text: Whether the canary has been running for at least one hour, regardless of the metrics it shows
options.explanation: Time alone does not show health.

options.text: Whether the developers like the new version
Whether the release was built on a Monday
Whether the canary uses less disk space
options.explanation: Disk usage is a minor signal.

options.text: Whether all tests were skipped

questions.question_text: A database schema change must be deployed with the application. What approach supports safe CD?

options.text: Use backward-compatible migrations (expand, migrate, contract) so old and new code can run together
Run destructive migrations first so the schema is clean, then deploy the new code afterwards
options.explanation: Old code may break immediately after a destructive migration.

options.text: Avoid schema changes entirely in continuous delivery
options.explanation: Schema changes are possible with careful patterns.

options.text: Deploy the code first and run migrations manually next month
Drop and recreate the database on each deployment
Edit production tables by hand during the release
options.explanation: Manual changes are error-prone and untracked.

questions.question_text: Your pipeline downloads dependencies from public registries. What practice best reduces supply-chain risk?

options.text: Pin versions, verify integrity hashes and use a trusted internal mirror
options.explanation: These controls block unexpected or tampered packages.

options.text: Always use the latest versions to get security fixes automatically
options.explanation: Unpinned latest versions can introduce malicious updates.

options.text: Public registries are always safe because packages are reviewed
options.explanation: Public packages are not systematically reviewed.

options.text: Download dependencies manually on developer laptops
Disable dependency caching
options.explanation: Caching is not the main risk.

options.text: Remove the lock file to simplify builds
options.explanation: Lock files are part of reproducibility.

questions.question_text: Which metric best shows how often a team successfully releases to production?

options.text: Deployment frequency
options.explanation: It is one of the DORA delivery metrics.

options.text: Lead time for changes
options.explanation: That measures time from commit to production, not frequency.

options.text: Lines of code written per week
options.explanation: Code volume is not a delivery metric.

options.text: Number of open pull requests
Number of CI servers
Code coverage percentage

questions.question_text: On a circuit diagram, what does a straight line between two components represent?

options.text: A conductor that electrically connects them
options.explanation: Lines show wires or traces with negligible resistance.

options.text: A conductor, but only when it is drawn in red
options.explanation: Line colour is not part of the electrical meaning in standard schematics.

options.text: The physical length and route of the cable in the building
options.explanation: Schematics show connections, not physical routing or length.

options.text: A resistor with a very small value
A boundary between two separate circuits
options.explanation: Boundaries are drawn with dashed outlines or notes, not plain wires.

options.text: The direction in which current is not allowed to flow
options.explanation: Plain lines do not restrict current direction.

questions.question_text: Two wires cross on a schematic with no dot at the crossing. What does that usually mean?

options.text: The wires are not connected
options.explanation: By convention, a junction is marked with a dot.

options.text: The wires are connected, because any crossing is a junction
options.explanation: Only crossings marked with a dot are junctions in common practice.

options.text: The wires are connected only if they carry the same voltage
options.explanation: Voltage does not decide connection on a drawing.

options.text: One of the wires is broken at that point
options.explanation: A crossing does not indicate a break.

options.text: The wires must be twisted together during installation
options.explanation: Installation details are not shown that way.

options.text: The crossing marks the location of a fuse

questions.question_text: Which symbol property identifies the positive terminal of a battery on most schematics?

options.text: The longer plate line
options.explanation: The longer line indicates the positive terminal.

options.text: The shorter plate line
options.explanation: The shorter line is the negative terminal.

options.text: The terminal drawn closest to the top of the page
options.explanation: Orientation on the page does not define polarity.

options.text: The terminal connected to the ground symbol
options.explanation: Ground can connect to either terminal depending on the circuit.

options.text: The thicker wire leaving the battery
options.explanation: Wire thickness on a drawing is not a polarity marker.

options.text: The terminal labelled with the battery's voltage
options.explanation: The voltage label describes the cell, not the terminal.

questions.question_text: What is the purpose of the ground symbol on a schematic?

options.text: To mark the common reference point for voltages in the circuit
options.explanation: Ground is the 0 V reference used by the circuit.

options.text: To show the point where the circuit must be connected to earth in every design
options.explanation: Signal ground is a reference and is not always tied to earth.

options.text: To show where excess current is thrown away safely
options.explanation: Ground is a reference node, not a dump for current.

options.text: To show a component that stores charge
To mark the end of the drawing sheet
options.explanation: Sheet borders are shown with frames.

options.text: To show where the circuit is switched off

questions.question_text: What does a reference designator like R12 or C3 on a schematic indicate?

options.text: A unique label linking the symbol to a specific part in the bill of materials
options.explanation: Designators map symbols to physical components.

options.text: The value of the part written in short form, such as 12 ohms for R12 or 3 farads for C3
options.explanation: Values are written separately from the designator.

options.text: The order in which the parts must be soldered
options.explanation: Designators are identifiers, not assembly order.

options.text: The page number where the part appears
The power rating of the component
options.explanation: Ratings are listed in the BOM or as notes.

options.text: The supplier part number
options.explanation: Supplier numbers are in the BOM.

questions.question_text: A schematic shows a net label "VCC_3V3" at several places with no wire drawn between them. What does this mean?

options.text: All points with the same net label are electrically connected
options.explanation: Net labels connect nodes without drawing long wires.

options.text: They are connected, but only if the labels are on the same sheet
options.explanation: Global labels or ports often connect across sheets, depending on the tool.

options.text: They are separate supplies that happen to have the same voltage
options.explanation: Identical labels mean the same net.

options.text: They are test points with no electrical function
The label is only a comment for the reader
options.explanation: Tools use net labels for connectivity.

options.text: They need to be connected by jumpers later
options.explanation: The schematic already defines the connection.

questions.question_text: Why are decoupling capacitors placed near integrated circuits in a schematic and layout?

options.text: To supply local current and filter high-frequency noise on the power pins
To store energy for the whole board, so placement does not matter
options.explanation: Distance adds inductance and reduces effectiveness.

options.text: To block DC voltage from reaching the IC
options.explanation: Decoupling capacitors are connected between supply and ground, not in series.

options.text: To increase the clock frequency of the IC
options.explanation: Capacitors do not raise clock speed.

options.text: To protect the IC against reverse polarity
options.explanation: That needs a diode or protection circuit.

options.text: To act as pull-up resistors

questions.question_text: In a hierarchical schematic, what is the advantage of sheet symbols or blocks?

options.text: They split a large design into reusable, readable sub-circuits
They reduce the number of components that must be purchased
options.explanation: Hierarchy affects drawing structure, not part count.

options.text: They automatically make the circuit more power efficient
options.explanation: Drawing structure does not change circuit behaviour.

options.text: They prevent connections between different sheets
They are required for single-layer PCBs only
options.explanation: Hierarchy is independent of board layers.

options.text: They convert analogue circuits to digital
options.explanation: Hierarchy does not change circuit type.

questions.question_text: An electrical rule check (ERC) reports "output pin connected to output pin." Why is this a concern?

options.text: Two outputs driving the same net can fight and damage the drivers
options.explanation: Conflicting outputs can cause excessive current.

options.text: It is only a warning about drawing style and can always be ignored
options.explanation: Some cases, such as open-drain outputs, are acceptable, but it must be reviewed.

options.text: Outputs must always be connected to other outputs to share load
options.explanation: Normal push-pull outputs should not be paralleled.

options.text: The ERC cannot read pin directions
The two pins are on different sheets
options.explanation: Sheet location is not the issue.

options.text: The pins have different reference designators

questions.question_text: When reading a motor control schematic, what does a normally open (NO) contact mean?

options.text: The contact is open when the device is not energised and closes when it is activated
The contact is open while the motor is running and closes again when the motor stops
options.explanation: The state depends on the actuating device, not the motor.
